problems.description: In route_message, message.get("type") is evaluated before the isinstance(message, dict) guard, so a client that sends a valid base64-JSON non-dict (e.g. an array) makes the handler raise AttributeError outside the decode try/except, killing that connection.

decode_message's except tuple lists json.JSONDecodeError and base64.binascii.Error, both subclasses of ValueError, so the tuple is redundant; also base64.binascii relies on an implicit import side-effect rather than an explicit binascii import.

Two measured convention violations in test_notification_server.py (Classes should use PascalCase; module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) — the only violations attributable to this commit, in the truncated tail of the test file.

strengths: Exactly matches the Session 1 greenfield spec: websockets library (not Flask-SocketIO), asyncio, thread-safe ClientRegistry (threading.Lock), uuid client IDs, broadcast/direct/system routing, and GET /health returning the client count.
Clean layering — connection registry concerns separated from routing/transport concerns, with encode_message/decode_message isolating the base64 wire format.
Modern websockets.asyncio.server API with process_request for the REST endpoint; consistent type hints, docstrings, and from __future__ import annotations.
No new bugs and 0.0% duplication; tests cover the connect handshake, broadcast, direct delivery, and health polling with proper timeouts.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-compliant greenfield Session 1 implementation — measured convention score 0.78 is dominated by violations in files (app.py, transports.py, later-session tests) that are NOT part of this commit, so the commit's own code is near-conforming, with only the trivial route_message guard-ordering bug and two minor test-file naming violations standing out.

problems.description: SonarQube measured cognitive complexity +27 in +105 lines; route_message now nests channel extraction ahead of broadcast/direct dispatch, making the routing logic significantly harder to follow.
New subscribe/unsubscribe message types and three REST endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers) ship with zero test coverage (AST diff: +0 files).

Channel-presence check in route_message runs before the direct/broadcast branches, so a 'direct' message that happens to carry a channel field is silently re-routed to channel subscribers instead of its target.

Introduces a second lock (_sub_lock) and a parallel _subscriptions structure duplicating client/subscription lifecycle that overlaps the existing registry; safe today (locks are never nested) but a deadlock hazard if acquisition order changes.

Convention score 0.78 is driven by 8 pre-existing violations in app.py, test_*.py, and transports.py — all files untouched by this commit; the +105 lines added to notification_server.py are convention-clean.
/channels/{name}/subscribers returns 200 with an empty list for an unknown channel rather than 404, inconsistent with the health/channels resource semantics.

strengths: Mirrors existing patterns faithfully: subscribe/unsubscribe handled in the established type-dispatch flow, REST endpoints appended alongside /health, and disconnect cleanup wired into handler's finally block.
Subscription state is lock-protected and snapshots are returned sorted, avoiding mutation-during-iteration races in send_to_channel.
send_to_channel reuses the codebase's error-handling idiom (drop dead clients on send failure), keeping channel delivery consistent with broadcast.
All new code in notification_server.py is convention-clean: snake_case methods, PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE SUPPORTED_TYPES.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-patterned channel-subscription feature that respects existing architecture and introduces no new convention violations, but carries real debt via +27 cognitive complexity and entirely untested new routing/endpoints.

problems.description: Two sources of truth for connected clients: local thread-safe ClientRegistry vs RedisBus.CLIENTS_SET via register_client/unregister_client — state can drift between local and Redis views, and it is unclear which is authoritative for routing decisions.
Lazy `import redis.asyncio` inside RedisBus._get_client hides the dependency and breaks top-level import clarity; prefer importing redis.asyncio explicitly or standardizing the injection point.

8 convention violations (Classes should use PascalCase, Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) in test_notification_server.py, test_rate_limit_history.py, test_redis_integration.py, app.py, and transports.py, consistent with the measured convention score of 0.78.
Cognitive complexity +43 with the new conditional Redis-on/Redis-off execution paths (bus may be None, _pubsub/_worker_task may be unset), which complicates the server lifecycle.
MessageStore opens a fresh SQLite connection per operation rather than reusing a connection or pool — acceptable at this scale but will not scale with load.

strengths: Redis pub/sub backbone and SQLite history are cleanly separated into focused classes (RedisBus, MessageStore) with single responsibilities.
Redis client is injectable and lazily activated, keeping the server usable without Redis while enabling cross-instance distribution and easy test seams.
Solid SQLite hygiene: parameterized queries (no injection), sqlite3.Row accessors, contextlib.closing, and json.dumps payload serialization.
Explicit lifecycle management (start()/worker task creation) and documented envelope semantics in the module docstring.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration commit that cleanly separates Redis backbone and SQLite persistence into focused classes, but introduces dual client-state bookkeeping (architecture debt), a hidden lazy redis import, and 8 convention violations (score 0.78) that keep it neutral overall.

problems.description: ClientRegistry and handler replace the concrete ServerConnection type with Any, trading away static type safety; a Protocol or TypeVar for the transport's connection type would preserve it.

create_transport(transport, self) injects the server into the transport factory, creating a bidirectional coupling where the transport's handle() calls back into NotificationServer methods; a narrower callback/interface would decouple them.
transports.py introduces new module-level constants that violate UPPER_CASE naming (per mechanical scan). Most other listed violations are pre-existing in test files/app.py, not introduced here.
Cognitive complexity +2 is a mild increase from the transport dispatch indirection; acceptable for the abstraction gained.

strengths: Clean single-responsibility extraction of the transport layer; handler() collapses to a thin delegate and the WebSocket specifics move to transports.py
Reduces duplication (-0.6%) and exposes a clear public API via __all__
Backward compatible — defaults to the WebSocket transport and follows the existing env-var configuration pattern (TRANSPORT alongside REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL)
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, backward-compatible transport-layer extraction that improves separation of concerns and reduces duplication, at the cost of minor type-safety regressions (Any) and a small new convention slip in transports.py.

problems.description: 8 convention violations measured (score 0.78): non-PascalCase classes and non-UPPER_CASE module-level constants in test_rate_limit_history.py, test_redis_integration.py, test_notification_server.py, app.py, and transports.py. Flag: the shown notification_server.py diff itself is convention-clean (_int_env snake_case, RateLimiter PascalCase, CLEANUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS UPPER_CASE, __all__ updated) — the violations sit mostly in the newly-added test files plus pre-existing app.py/transports.py, so the 0.78 reflects whole-repo state rather than this diff alone.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +40 and +2 smells across the rate-limit/history/cleanup additions; query_history partially re-implements the existing list() SELECT with its own clause-building, duplicating the payload-decode row mapping.

delete_older_than compares timestamps lexicographically via `timestamp < cutoff`; safe only because utc_now() writes uniform UTC ISO strings, but silently retains stale rows if a naive or differently-offset timestamp is ever persisted.

RateLimiter limit/window_seconds are typed `Any` with runtime int coercion; Optional[int] would be clearer, and the truncated _cleanup_loop/_handle_message wiring could not be inspected for error handling.

strengths: Rate limiter uses Redis INCR+EXPIRE fixed-window with a time.monotonic in-memory fallback, preserving the codebase's 'keep working without Redis' pattern and degrading safely on Redis errors.
Clean lifecycle symmetry: the background cleanup task is started in start() and cancelled/awaited in stop(), mirroring the existing _worker_task pattern.
Blocking SQLite deletes are offloaded with asyncio.to_thread; query_history uses parameterized SQL with the limit+1 has_more pagination idiom.
Configuration is injected via constructor params with _int_env fallback, and RateLimiter is added to __all__ as an explicit public export.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitting cross-cutting session that adds rate limiting, history pagination, and TTL cleanup following the server's existing Redis+fallback, asyncio-lifecycle, and env-config patterns, with only minor convention debt concentrated in the new test files and modest added complexity.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (app.py, a Flask Todo API) is entirely unrelated to the notification service and is abandoned after Session 1 — orphaned dead code persists through all 5 sessions
Bytecode artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc) are committed from Session 1 onward because the Session 3 .gitignore only excludes *.db/*.sqlite, not __pycache__
Session 1's base64 wire-encoding and single-file layout survived as a legacy constraint, forcing Session 4's extraction of the transport layer and leaving base64 encoding as a hard-wired default
Session 3's route_message duplicates delivery logic between the Redis-publish path and the local path, so delivery semantics must be maintained in two places
Session 1's route_message calls message.get('type') before the isinstance(message, dict) guard, making the guard dead code
key_decisions: Greenfield rebuild (Session 1): discarded the Flask Todo seed and built a standalone WebSocket notification server with a base64-encoded JSON envelope wire protocol
In-process channel subscription registry behind a dedicated lock (Session 2) — subscription state kept local rather than pushed to the broker

Redis pub/sub backbone with a background delivery worker, Redis-stored client state, and SQLite MessageStore persistence, all with in-memory/local fallbacks so the server works without Redis (Session 3)
Pluggable BaseTransport abstraction selected by the TRANSPORT env var, decoupling connection handling from the routing core (Session 4)
Redis-or-in-memory RateLimiter, a /history query API with pagination, and a background TTL cleanup loop (Session 5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 delivered a minimal single-file server with 9 passing tests; Session 2 added channels cleanly; Session 3 was the riskiest step (743s, 48 tool calls, 4 retries, a temporary agentic test dip) as Redis + persistence were layered in; Session 4 consolidated with a clean transport extraction that kept all 16 tests green; Session 5 capped the build with rate limiting, history, and TTL cleanup, growing coverage to 25 tests. Code grew 313→996 lines and tests 166→643, with all sessions passing, confidence 1.0 throughout, and no cascade recovery triggered even under the early-degrade perturbation.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental build — greenfield WebSocket server, channels, Redis integration, transport refactor, then cross-cutting rate limiting/history — where each session composes on the prior one and the test suite stays green while growing from 9 to 25 tests.
